title: Law of Conservation of Mass â€” Statement
notes: **Statement:** matter (mass) can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction â€” the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products
This is why chemical equations must be balanced: the same total mass, and the same number of each type of atom, must appear on both sides

**Statement:** a given chemical compound always contains its constituent elements combined together in the same fixed proportion by mass, regardless of the source of the compound or the method used to prepare it
This is verified experimentally by checking that the percentage composition of an element stays constant across independently prepared samples of the same compound
**Statement:** when two elements combine to form more than one compound, the different masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other element are in a ratio of small whole numbers
This is verified by finding the mass of one element that combines with a fixed mass (e.g. 1 g) of the other element in each compound, then comparing those masses as a ratio

**Statement:** when two different elements combine separately with a fixed mass of a third element, the ratio of the masses in which they do so is either the same as, or a simple whole-number multiple of, the ratio of masses in which the two elements combine directly with each other

This is verified by finding (i) the mass of each of the two elements that combines with a fixed mass of the third element (in two separate compounds), and (ii) the actual ratio of those two elements in a compound where they combine directly â€” then comparing the two ratios

**Step 1 â€” divide by the smallest value:** take the calculated list of masses (or mass ratios), pick the smallest one, and divide every value in the list by it â€” this forces the smallest value to become exactly 1

**Step 2 â€” clear any remaining decimals:** if a result still ends in .5, .33/.66, or .25/.75, multiply every value in the list by a common factor to clear it â€” Ã—2 for .5, Ã—3 for .33/.66, Ã—4 for .25/.75 â€” until all values are whole numbers
